nameStory: The Propellerclam gets its distinctive name from its peculiar shell shape - when viewed from the side, it looks remarkably like an old-fashioned boat propeller! The elongated, twisted shell with its characteristic gape at both ends creates that unmistakable propeller silhouette that makes this clam easy to remember once you've seen one.
description: The Propellerclam is a large, unusual-looking saltwater clam that lives buried in muddy sea bottoms along New England's coast. Its shell is distinctively elongated and somewhat twisted, with a chalky white to grayish color and prominent growth rings. These clams can grow quite large, reaching up to 4-5 inches in length, making them one of the more substantial bivalves you might encounter. Unlike many clams, their shells don't close completely - they always have gaps at both ends where the siphons extend.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Distinctively elongated and slightly twisted shell that resembles a boat propeller when viewed from the side, with the shell never fully closing at either end

idTips.label: Color and Texture
idTips.description: Chalky white to light gray shell surface that feels rough and powdery to the touch, often with a slightly dull finish rather than glossy

idTips.label: Growth Rings
idTips.description: Prominent concentric ridges or rings across the shell surface that you can feel with your fingertip, creating a ribbed texture

idTips.label: Shell Gaps
idTips.description: Permanent openings at both ends of the shell where the dark siphons protrude - the shell literally cannot close completely

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large for a New England clam, typically 3-5 inches long, feeling substantial and heavy in your hand

habitat: Propellerclams live buried deep in soft mud and clay bottoms in cold, deeper coastal waters from the low tide zone down to considerable depths. In New England, they're most commonly found in areas with fine sediments in protected bays and sounds, particularly in northern Maine waters where conditions remain consistently cold. You're most likely to encounter empty shells washed up on beaches rather than finding live specimens, as they burrow 6-12 inches deep in the seafloor.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms, appearing bright white and chalky. This is often the best time to find intact specimens on beaches as wave action increases.
seasonality.summer: Beach finds become less common as calmer seas mean fewer shells wash ashore, but this is when live specimens are most active in deeper waters.
seasonality.fall: Storm season brings more shells to shore, though they may be more weathered and gray. Look for them mixed in with other storm debris along the high tide line.
seasonality.winter: Harsh winter storms can bring up specimens from deeper waters, but shells may be heavily worn and harder to identify due to prolonged wave action.

funFact: Propellerclams are incredibly long-lived - some specimens have been aged at over 100 years old! They grow extremely slowly in the frigid northern waters, adding just a tiny bit to their shell each year, which means that large specimen you find on the beach could have been alive when your great-grandparents were children.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with large razor clams, but Propellerclams are much wider and have that distinctive twisted, propeller-like shape rather than the straight, narrow 'razor' profile. Remember: if it looks like it could spin through water like a boat propeller, you've found the right clam!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'rock-borer,' Propellerclams don't actually bore into solid rock like some of their family members - they're adapted for deep burrowing in soft sediments instead. The family name can be misleading when applied to this particular species.
compareHints: Since Propellerclams are the only species in their genus found in New England waters, compare them to other large burrowing clams in the rock-borer family. Unlike the smaller, rounder Hiatella species that actually do bore into hard surfaces, Propellerclams are much larger, more elongated, and adapted for deep mud rather than hard substrate. Their distinctive propeller shape and large size make them quite unique among New England's marine bivalves.
